name: Carla Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Carla. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm charge hand for Fairway Interiors, which means I run the carpentry side on shop and office fit-outs. This month it's a dentist's surgery in an old bank on the high street: metal stud partitions, fire doors, a reception desk we're building on site. I start at seven thirty, check deliveries, set out the walls with a laser level, then work alongside the other three till four or so. Shops want everything done at night sometimes, so I do a fair few late shifts too.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the finish. On a new build nobody sees your work behind the plasterboard, but in a fit-out the door I hang is the door the dentist walks through every day. What wears me out is the late nights and the pay. Fairway pays below the city firms, and there are only two fit-out companies in town, so moving doesn't get you much. My partner Dev drives a delivery van, and between us we just about cover rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it turned out to be a handy extra, not a big deal. Probably make a joke at the site cabin about all the people who said we'd be replaced by now. That's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it means the same as now. Not great pay, but steady work. I could live with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on at Fairway. Try to put fifty a month aside, which is the plan every year and works about half the time. Maybe push for a rise if a bigger contract comes in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Same worries I already have, nothing new on top.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use AI now and then. For what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Checking building regs, mainly. Like, what fire rating does this door need in a medical building. It gives me a straight answer quicker than wading through the documents, then I check it with the site manager. Sometimes I use it to make a materials list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing changes, what are you and Dev aiming for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A deposit, one day. Maybe kids in a few years, not yet. We've got about three weeks of money between us, so it's a long road, but we'd keep walking it.

S0.say: I'd say it turned out to be a handy extra, not a big deal. I'd make a joke in the site cabin about everyone who said we'd be replaced by now.
S0.think: It means the same as now for me. Not great pay, but steady work, and I could live with that.
S0.do: Carries on at Fairway and aims to save 50 a month, which she admits works about half the time. Pushes for a rise if a larger contract comes in.
S0.feel: Calm, with the same worries she already has and nothing new on top.
S0.quote: Try to put fifty a month aside, which is the plan every year and works about half the time.
S0.fieldNote: Carla is pragmatic and honest about her own habits, including failing to save. She uses AI for quick regulation checks but always confirms them with a person. Her household runs on two low incomes and a shared long-term goal of a deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say you have to roll with it. Learn what's useful, ignore the rest. That's what I'd tell the younger ones on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm more worried about Dev than me. Self-driving vans feel closer than robots hanging fire doors. If his money goes, mine alone doesn't pay the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get better at the AI stuff for planning and ordering, because the charge hand who runs a tight job keeps her place. I'd look at what training Fairway might pay for. And we'd try harder to save, maybe a hundred a month, so we'd have a buffer if Dev's hours get cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A worry at the back of my head, mostly about him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Dev. How exposed is his job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: His company's already trialling vans that drive themselves on the motorway part. He says a person still has to carry the parcel to the door. For now. He says it like a joke, but he's checked the job ads twice this month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What part of your own work do you think goes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Setting out, probably. Those robots that draw the walls on the floor from the plans are already out there. And the metal stud walls, they're very repetitive. Hanging doors in an old bank where nothing's level, I think that lasts longer.

S1.say: I'd say you have to roll with it: learn what's useful and ignore the rest. That's what I'd tell the younger ones on site.
S1.think: I'm more worried about Dev than me, because self-driving vans feel closer than robots hanging fire doors. If his money goes, mine alone doesn't pay the rent.
S1.do: Gets better at AI planning and ordering tools and asks what training Fairway would fund. Tries to raise household saving to about 100 a month in case her partner's hours are cut.
S1.feel: Uneasy, mostly on her partner's behalf.
S1.quote: He says it like a joke, but he's checked the job ads twice this month.
S1.fieldNote: Carla's main exposure runs through her partner rather than herself. She sees which parts of her own job are repetitive enough to go, like setting out and stud walls. Her plan is moderate and practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody could have prepared for that, so the government has to help people get through it. I'm not a protest person, but I'd sign things and I'd vote for whoever had an actual plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it'd be both of us at once. Dev's van and my walls. With three weeks of money, that's not a dip, it's a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd cut everything straight away: no car on finance, his phone contract, eating out, all gone. I'd look for any work that needs a person on site, maybe snagging and repairs for the robot firms. And we'd put the house and the kids talk on hold completely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be doing the maths every night and not liking the answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Dev actually change at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably move somewhere cheaper, a smaller flat, maybe share with his brother. We'd stop talking about a deposit. That's the bit that would hurt, giving up on the plan rather than the money itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd take anything. What's the line you wouldn't cross?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't take something unsafe, like signing off work I haven't checked. I've seen what happens with bad fire doors. Apart from that, anything. Night shifts, weekend work, driving, cleaning, I'm not proud.

S2.say: I'd say nobody could prepare for that, so the government has to help people through it. I'd sign things and vote for whoever had a real plan.
S2.think: It would hit both of us at once, Dev's van and my walls. With three weeks of money that's not a dip, it's a cliff.
S2.do: Cuts household spending immediately, from the car finance to the phone contract. Looks for any on-site work such as snagging and repairs, and puts the house and children plans on hold.
S2.feel: Alarmed, doing the maths each night and not liking the answer.
S2.quote: With three weeks of money, that's not a dip, it's a cliff.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture hits Carla through two incomes at once. What she would grieve most is giving up the shared plan, not the money. She draws one firm line, on safety, and is open to any other work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready, so let's get ready. Retraining, help with bills while people learn. Sensible stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it gives us a chance. Not a comfortable one, but a chance. I'd want to get moving in the first year, not the fourth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a fire safety inspection course at the college, evenings, in the first year. Keep working at Fairway and use the AI tools more to run jobs faster. We'd push the savings to a hundred a month and hold off on kids till we know where we stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's an anxious with a plan attached.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why fire safety?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I already know fire doors and partitions inside out. Somebody still has to check that a building's safe, and people will want a person to blame if it goes wrong, not a robot. That sounds grim, but it's true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Dev retrain too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's talked about getting his electrician's qualification for years. Maybe this is what finally makes him do it. One of us studying at a time, though, we can't afford both.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to get ready, so let's get ready. Retraining and help with bills while people learn, sensible things.
S3.think: It gives us a chance, not a comfortable one, but a chance. I'd want to move in the first year, not the fourth.
S3.do: Starts an evening fire safety inspection course in the first year while staying at Fairway. Uses AI tools to run jobs faster, raises saving to about 100 a month and delays having children.
S3.feel: Anxious, but with a plan attached.
S3.quote: People will want a person to blame if it goes wrong, not a robot.
S3.fieldNote: Carla picks a retraining path that builds on what she already knows, fire doors and partitions. Her reasoning about blame and responsibility was sharp and unsentimental. She and her partner would take turns studying because they can't afford both at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time, let's not waste it. Ten years is a long time to plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fine in ten years. But I don't think Dev's van job lasts ten years, so we'd feel it long before the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the fire safety course, probably starting in year two once we've got a bit saved. Keep at Fairway. Help Dev get on the electrician course first, because his clock is shorter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, honestly. Less than the others, but there's a long squeeze in the middle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Dev's job might go before yours, even in the ten-year one. Why does that matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the end point is ten years off, but our money problem might be three years off. If he's out of work in year three, I'm paying everything on a low wage for years. That's the real worry, not 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you have kids in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, later on. If I'm qualified and he's working, then yes. I'd want to know there's a job for at least one of us that a robot isn't going to do.

S4.say: I'd say we have time, so let's not waste it. Ten years is a long time to plan.
S4.think: I'd probably be fine in ten years, but I don't think Dev's van job lasts that long. We'd feel it long before the end.
S4.do: Helps her partner start an electrician course first because his job is more exposed, then begins her fire safety course around year two. Stays at Fairway and plans children only once one of them is qualified.
S4.feel: Anxious, less than in the other AGI pictures, because of a long squeeze in the middle.
S4.quote: The end point is ten years off, but our money problem might be three years off.
S4.fieldNote: Even with ten years, Carla stays anxious because her household's weak point comes early, through her partner's driving job. She would put his retraining first. This was a good example of how a household, not just a job, sets the timeline.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Both of us out at once, no money, no time. What would help is something to cover the rent while people retrain, and courses you can do at night so you can keep working. And honest information about which jobs are actually safe, because everyone's guessing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about partners. Everybody gets asked about their own job, but half of what worries me is Dev's. Families sink or swim together.

headlineQuote: Hanging doors in an old bank where nothing's level, I think that lasts longer.
portrait: Carla is a 27-year-old charge hand on shop and office fit-outs, living with her partner Dev, a delivery driver, on about three weeks of shared savings. She uses AI now and then to check building regulations, always confirming with a person. Her worry runs through Dev's job as much as her own: she is calm if AI fizzles, uneasy as self-driving vans arrive, and alarmed when AGI in two years would hit both incomes at once. With five or ten years she would retrain as a fire safety inspector and put family plans on hold, staying anxious because her household's money problem comes years before the end point.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because both she and her partner would lose work at once with no money and no time.
whatWouldHelp: Rent support while people retrain, evening courses so people can keep working, and honest information about which jobs are really safe.
